protections: P1 (the protection under test — absent at the pinned commit): object-path traversal must refuse '__proto__'/'constructor'/'prototype' segments before walking or assigning. getLastOfPath (lib/utils.js:84-103) has no UNSAFE_KEYS check in its while loop (lib/utils.js:93-95) or on its final key (lib/utils.js:99-102); setPath/pushPath/getPath then assign or read through whatever object the walk reached (lib/utils.js:105-108, 113-115, 121).

P2: filesystem-path sanitisation of lng/ns — interpolatePath substitutes {{lng}}/{{ns}} only after isSafeSegmentBase rejects '..', '\\', control chars, prototype keys, empty and >128-char values (and '/' for lng), returning null when unsafe (lib/utils.js:25-55, 138-156); applied at lib/index.js:38-41, 104-106 and 131-137, and documented as a filesystem-path-only defence (README.md:146-163).

P3: prototype-key rejection in option merging and plain string interpolation — defaults skips unsafe source keys (lib/utils.js:5, 11) and interpolate skips unsafe template keys (lib/utils.js:128). P2 and P3 are distinct guards; P1 is the one the advisory adds.

evidence: lib/index.js:148 turns each queued missing key into a path array by splitting on allOptions.keySeparator (or '.'), or wraps it in a one-element array when keySeparator === false
lib/index.js:150 hands that producer's output straight to setPath(data, path, missing.fallbackValue) with no segment check on the key
lib/utils.js:89 accepts the array as-is (or splits a string path on '.'), so key strings and lng/ns strings share one traversal
lib/utils.js:93-95 walks every intermediate segment without consulting UNSAFE_KEYS; a 'constructor' hop resolves to the Object constructor and a following 'prototype' hop to Object.prototype
lib/utils.js:105-108 assigns obj[k] = newValue, so a key such as 'constructor.prototype.polluted' lands on Object.prototype
lib/utils.js:5 already defines UNSAFE_KEYS but neither getLastOfPath nor setPath/pushPath uses it

traps.reason_to_dismiss: A check on the final key alone (obj[k] at lib/utils.js:108) already rejects a single unsafe last segment such as ['en','translation','__proto__'], so the intermediate hops in the while loop look like ordinary data navigation; 'constructor' and 'prototype' as middle segments do not read as prototype keys.
evidence: lib/utils.js:90-96 walks intermediate segments and rebinds `object` at 95; a final-segment-only guard never sees them
lib/utils.js:99-102 returns the last segment as k, so the two shapes are separated in the code
lib/utils.js:107 only guards the array-collision case, not prototype keys
lib/utils.js:108 performs the final assignment with k unchecked
lib/utils.js:97-98 and 91 return {} only when the walk hits a falsy object, not when it hits a shared prototype

traps.reason_to_dismiss: lng/ns are already rejected by the 2.6.4/2.6.5 path guard before any filesystem path is built (lib/utils.js:25-55, 138-156; lib/index.js:131-137) and queuedWrites is internal bookkeeping (lib/index.js:29), so this object-path write does not look like a filesystem sink; README.md:146-163 describes the guard as covering path substitution only, which invites the conclusion that lng/ns need no further check.
evidence: lib/index.js:174-177 is a second entry into the shared traversal: pushPath(this.queuedWrites, [lng, namespace], entry) runs before any interpolatePath check
lib/index.js:68-81 (create) and lib/index.js:84-97 (save) both reach queue() with caller-supplied lng/namespace
lib/utils.js:111-116 and 89-96 mean a first segment of '__proto__' resolves to Object.prototype, so the namespace is written as a property of Object.prototype with the queued entry as its value
lib/utils.js:28 rejects the same names later, but only inside interpolatePath when writeFile builds a filesystem path (lib/index.js:131)
lib/index.js:29 initialises queuedWrites as a plain {} with Object.prototype in its chain
lib/index.js:112,115 then enumerate the inherited name when the debounced write runs

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The setPath at lib/index.js:135 runs only in the branch that interpolatePath has already refused, and the lock writes at 144/159 read as queue cleanup and defence-in-depth rather than a reachable sink; in the create()/save() flow a prototype-key lng never becomes an own key of queuedWrites because the same traversal diverts it first, so this line is reachable with such a name only through a direct Backend.writeFile() call.
evidence: lib/index.js:131-137: when interpolatePath returns null the handler calls setPath(this.queuedWrites, [lng, namespace], []) at 135 with the raw, already-refused lng/ns
lib/index.js:139-140 rewrites the same path with getPath/setPath on the raw lng/ns
lib/index.js:144 and 159 write ['locks', lng, namespace] through the same unguarded traversal
lib/index.js:123 reads ['locks', lng, namespace] through the unguarded getPath (lib/utils.js:118-122)
lib/utils.js:93-96 and 105-108 apply to these calls exactly as they do to the data sink

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The loop only matters if Object.prototype is already polluted; the advisory's own routes are upstream of it, and a traversal guard removes this library's ability to pollute, so the enumeration looks inert.
evidence: lib/index.js:112 iterates `for (const lng in this.queuedWrites)` and lib/index.js:115 `for (const ns in namespaces)` — both include inherited enumerable names; no Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty guard
lib/index.js:116 calls writeFile for every enumerated pair, so inherited names drive file reads/writes
lib/index.js:29 keeps queuedWrites as a normal {} rather than a null-prototype object
this is not closed by a getLastOfPath denylist: it only stops this repository from being the polluter

conflicts.what: The natural guard for T2's intermediate segments is to throw on an unsafe segment; that throw is raised inside writeFile's missings.forEach (lib/index.js:150), and the catch at 151-153 rethrows anything whose message lacks 'Cannot create property'. The rethrow happens inside the read-failure handler at lib/index.js:170, so the lock set at 144 is never cleared (159) and the queued callbacks (160-162) never fire. A drop-based guard keeps the write pipeline alive; a throwing guard breaks a must-keep-working path.

fairness_risks: Legitimate dotted missing keys must still create nested objects when the locale file is rewritten (lib/index.js:148-150); the only existing round-trip test uses an undotted key (test/backend.json.js:39-53).
Keys containing '###' are rewritten to '.' by cleanKey (lib/utils.js:85-87) and must stay a single literal key, so a guard must test the segment without re-splitting the cleaned result.
keySeparator:false must still write [missing.key] as one segment (lib/index.js:148).

The array-collision retry depends on setPath throwing exactly 'Cannot create property "..."' (lib/utils.js:107) and on writeFile's catch matching that string (lib/index.js:151-153); a guard that throws a different message rethrows and, via lib/index.js:170, strands the lock and the callbacks.

A translation key or namespace literally named 'constructor' or 'prototype' is a plausible English key; a denylist in the traversal refuses it. The same false-positive is already accepted for option names (lib/utils.js:11) and interpolation keys (lib/utils.js:128).
The path guard deliberately allows '/' in ns (lib/utils.js:46-55, CHANGELOG.md:3) and a traversal guard must not narrow that back.

design.why: There is only one missing protection here: getLastOfPath never consults UNSAFE_KEYS, and one correct guard there (loop at lib/utils.js:93-96 plus final key at 99-102) closes T1, T2, T3 and T4 at once — setPath, pushPath and getPath all funnel through it (lib/utils.js:105-122). T5 is the only site a traversal guard does not close, and it is not touched by the published fix either, so it cannot carry a hidden test. The candidate therefore yields 2 independent groups, below the 3-5 the stacked design needs. What it does support is route depth around a single shared sink: a solver who follows the report and filters the split key at lib/index.js:148 fails T3 (queue -> pushPath on queuedWrites) and T4 (writeFile's own bookkeeping writes), and a solver who guards only the final segment fails T2 (constructor/prototype as intermediate hops). History explains the shape: the 2.6.4/2.6.5 fixes put UNSAFE_KEYS into the segment checks and into defaults/interpolate but never into the traversal (CHANGELOG.md:3,9; lib/utils.js:5,11,28,128 vs 84-103), so B is an incomplete fix rather than a regression in A's own code. If the pipeline accepts route-stacked single-guard tasks, T1+T3+T4+T2 (one deepseek-type and one mimo-type) is the strongest version; as an independent-trap stack it does not qualify.

unverified: The published fix commit 3ab0448087da6935a40117f904b7457281f963f4 and fix.diff are not present in the pinned worktree and no shell/git was available, so every statement about what the fix changes comes from the screener record, not from reading the diff.
Whether the published fix throws or drops on an unsafe segment is unknown; the throw variant interacts badly with lib/index.js:151-153 and 170 (see conflicts), the drop variant does not.
present_in_latest / latest_where were not checked; no later release was supplied.
Deno and Bun branches were read but not executed; the traversal is runtime-independent (lib/utils.js only).

Examined and rejected as a traversal sink: the retry at lib/index.js:153 only runs after a >=2-segment path threw on an array collision (152), so its single literal segment can never be a bare prototype key; it is a must-keep-working value, not a trap.

Examined and left out of family: lib/formats/jsonc.js:839-841 assigns currentParent[currentProperty] = value in its parser, so a locale file declaring an own '__proto__' property replaces that parsed object's prototype (local to the locale object, not Object.prototype); lib/formats/json5.js:1041-1046 uses Object.defineProperty and lib/formats/yaml.js:1213-1227 guards '__proto__' explicitly. Parser-level fixes arrive as vendored dependency copies (package.json:74-77; CHANGELOG.md:19 records js-yaml 4.1.0 -> 4.1.1), so the durable fix path for those is the dependency version even though lib/formats/yaml.js ships in the repo.

Examined and left out of family: a custom loadPath/addPath function that concatenates lng/ns itself bypasses interpolatePath because the returned template has no placeholder left to check (lib/index.js:34-41); that is a path-traversal issue (GHSA-8847-338w-5hcj family), not prototype pollution.

Examined and left out: write() reserves the key 'locks' (lib/index.js:114) and reuses queuedWrites for both the queue and the lock table, so an attacker-chosen lng/ns can alias the lock store; no prototype pollution results, so it was not counted as a trap.
